newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul union rally attracts 50,000 workers.
newsitem.headline: Seoul union rally attracts 50,000 workers.

text.p: Tens of thousands of South Korean workers rallied in Seoul on Sunday calling for abolition or revision of restrictive labour laws and threatening all-out strike unless their demands are met, witnesses said.
Earlier, Labour Minister Jin Nyum said the government would overhaul controversial legislation curbing union power by the end of this year.
His comments followed a meeting of senior government and ruling New Korea Party officials to discuss legal revision.
A presidential commission on labour reform was formed in May to produce a blueprint on bringing South Korean labour practices into line with those of industrialised nations.
Last week, the commission said it had reached agreements on some labour issues such as lifting the ban on trade unions' political activity, but not on most other key labour issues.

Witnesses said more than 50,000 workers of the Federation of Korea Trade Unions, the country's largest labour organisation, staged a rally near the National Assembly and tried to break a police line during a protest in front of the assembly building.
According to labour ministry officials, the federation has 5,875 unions within it, with over 1.2 million union members.
About 5,000 riot policemen ringed the rally site but no violence was reported.

Union anger has been directed at laws that bar more than one union in each workplace, prevent third-party intervention in industrial disputes, prohibit civil servants and all teachers from joining unions, and introduced the lay-off system.
The federation said the government is biased towards big business groups to keep the country competitive.

South Korea is under pressure to liberalise its labour regulations as it prepares to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). It was invited into the Paris-based grouping in October.

Business leaders oppose giving unions more power as they cut costs to cope with an economic downturn. Belt-tightening measures, including shedding staff and curbing wage increases, have alarmed workers who have threatened industrial unrest.
South Korea's tough labour laws are a legacy of past military-backed governments.
